reports.text: ARCHIVE: The moment Baghdad fell in April 2003, Israeli leaders began pushing Washington to go after Syria next. They did not hide it. They said it in public, on the record, in Hebrew and English. April 15 2003: Sharon gave a high-profile interview to Yedioth Ahronoth. He said Syrian President Assad "is dangerous. His judgment is impaired." He claimed Assad had allowed Saddam to move military equipment into Syria before the war. Then Sharon listed his demands for the United States. Washington should put "very heavy" pressure on Syria to force Assad to: end support for Hamas and Islamic Jihad, push Iran Revolutionary Guards out of the Bekka valley in Lebanon, stop cooperating with Iran, remove Hezbollah from the Israeli-Lebanese border and replace it with the Lebanese army, and eliminate Hezbollah missiles aimed at Israel. Read that list again. Every single item is an Israeli demand. Not one is an American interest. And Sharon wanted the American president to deliver all of it. One high-ranking Israeli diplomat saw this and warned that Sharon should adopt a lower profile when offering advice about relations between Damascus and Washington. Sharon ignored him. He was not alone. Defense Minister Shaul Mofaz told Ma'ariv on April 14: "We have a long list of issues that we are thinking of demanding of the Syrians and it is appropriate that it should be done through the Americans." Through the Americans. He said it plainly. Israel demands. America delivers. Two weeks later Sharon national security adviser Ephraim Halevy came to Washington. He encouraged US officials to take what the Forward reporter Ori Nir called "decisive action" against Syria. He called Assad "irresponsible" and "brash." At a WINEP conference on May 3 he said Assad was "prone to bad influence" and "cannot be left to his old tricks." Then he added: "There are many measures short of war that can be employed to draw the fangs of the young, arrogant, and inexperienced president of Syria." The threat claims did not hold up either. Israel accused Syria of hiding Saddam WMD. Congressman Engel said: "It wouldn't surprise me if those weapons of mass destruction that we cannot find in Iraq wound up and are today in Syria." No such weapons were ever found. Israel ambassador to the UN suggested Syria had provided the truck for the August 2003 bombing of UN headquarters in Baghdad. Itamar Rabinovich, former Israeli ambassador to Washington, told Seymour Hersh he "wondered" if Syria had "advance information about the September 11th plot—and failed to warn the United States." There was little or no evidence for any of it. The Israeli strategist Yossi Alpher warned that from Israel perspective "Syria could do a lot of damage, a lot more than Iraq." Syria had fewer than nineteen million people and a defense budget 1/300th the size of the United States. The Washington Post reported in mid-April 2003 that Sharon and Mofaz were fueling the campaign against Syria by feeding the United States intelligence reports about Assad. My analysis is this is the imperialist mindset again. Israel took the Golan in 1967. Syria wants it back. Israel refuses to return it. So Israel decides Syria has to be destroyed as a state, not because Syria threatens America, but because Syria keeps the claim alive. Destroy the state and the claim dies with it. Then Israel gets an American president to do the destroying. Mofaz said it out loud: "It is appropriate that it should be done through the Americans." That is not a partnership. That is a patron-client relationship, and America is the client. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: The campaign to turn America against Syria did not start after 9/11. It started years earlier. And the same people were involved the whole time. 1996: the Clean Break report that Feith, Perle, and Wurmser wrote for Netanyahu already named Syria as a target. It called for Israel to reorder the entire Middle East. Syria was on the list. May 2000: Daniel Pipes and Ziad Abdelnour of the U.S. Committee for a Free Lebanon coauthored a report calling for the US to use military threats to force Syria out of Lebanon, get rid of its WMD, and stop supporting terrorism. The signatories included Elliott Abrams, Douglas Feith, Richard Perle, David Wurmser, and Congressman Eliot Engel. Engel is a core supporter of the USCFL and one of Israel closest allies in Congress. None of this got traction during the Clinton years because Israel was then committed to making peace with Syria. That changed when Sharon came to power in 2001. Spring 2002: AIPAC promoted legislation to formally place Syria on the "axis of evil." Engel introduced the Syria Accountability Act. It threatened sanctions unless Syria withdrew from Lebanon, gave up its WMD, and stopped supporting terrorism. It also called for Syria and Lebanon to take concrete steps to make peace with Israel. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported the bill was "framed by some of Israel best friends in Congress" and that its "most avid proponent in the administration" was Elliott Abrams. The Bush administration opposed the bill in spring 2002. Two reasons. It might undermine the push for the Iraq war. And it might make Damascus stop giving Washington intelligence about al Qaeda. Congress put it on the back burner. Then Baghdad fell in April 2003. The lobby renewed the campaign. And now they wanted regime change, not behavior change. Paul Wolfowitz: "there has got to be regime change in Syria." Richard Perle: the message to other regimes is a two-word message. "You're next." The Defense Policy Board headed by Perle pushed a hard line against Syria. John Bolton prepared to tell Congress in mid-July 2003 that Syria WMD programs were a serious threat and had to be dealt with soon. The CIA and other agencies objected. They said Bolton was inflating the danger. The administration blocked his testimony. Bolton went anyway in September and called Syria a growing threat. April 2003 op-ed barrage: Yossi Klein Halevi in the LA Times "Next, Turn the Screws on Syria." Frank Gaffney in the Washington Times calling for "whatever techniques are necessary—including military force—to effect behavior modification and/or regime change in Damascus." Zev Chafets in the New York Daily News "Terror-Friendly Syria Needs a Change, Too." Lawrence Kaplan in the New Republic saying Assad was a serious threat to America. Jed Babbin in National Review cited an "Israeli source" who said Israel military and intelligence were "convinced that Assad will take risks a prudent leader wouldn't." So Assad unpredictability is a danger. That is the argument. Engel reintroduced the bill on April 12 2003. Perle called for Congress to pass it three days later. Bush administration stalled it again. August 2003: Engel and a group of New York politicians and Jewish leaders met Sharon in his Jerusalem office for ninety minutes. Sharon complained the US was not pressuring Syria enough. He thanked Engel for sponsoring the bill. He made clear he strongly favored continuing efforts to push it in Congress. The following month Engel announced he was "fed up with the administration's maneuvering on Syria" and pushed the bill again. With AIPAC full support he rounded up votes. Bush could no longer hold Congress back. The bill passed 398 to 4 in the House and 89 to 4 in the Senate. Bush signed it December 12 2003. look at the timeline. 1996 Clean Break names Syria. 2000 Pipes report signed by Abrams, Feith, Perle, Wurmser, and Engel. 2002 AIPAC writes the bill, Engel introduces it. 2003 Sharon thanks Engel for it in person. Bush opposes it twice. It passes anyway by huge margins. Then Bush signs it. Who was actually driving this? Not the president. The lobby and a foreign leader. And the president of the United States could not stop them. That is the entire point of this book in one bill. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: Bush did not want to confront Syria. He signed the Syria Accountability Act on December 12 2003, but he did it on a Friday night. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency described it this way: "Bush signed the act on a Friday night, the time the administration reserves for activities it would rather not share with the public, and the White House statement on the subject was about as Ive gotta do this but I dont wanna as it gets." Even after signing, Bush emphasized he would go slowly in implementing it. By spring 2004 Congressman Engel and his colleagues were so frustrated with the foot dragging that they threatened a new, tougher version of the bill. Bush had good reasons to resist. The State Department and the CIA openly opposed the confrontation. They said it was strategically unwise. Bush himself instructed the Pentagon in mid-April 2003 not to plan for war against Syria. That was right when the US appeared to have just won a dramatic victory in Iraq and talk about striking Syria was filling the air. But the neoconservatives in the administration did not just want confrontation. They wanted to refuse Syria help against al Qaeda. Flynt Leverett, who worked for Bush in the White House, wrote: "Neoconservatives in the Office of the Secretary of Defense and the Office of the Vice President opposed accepting Syrian help, arguing that it might create a sense of indebtedness to Damascus and inhibit an appropriate American response to a state sponsor of terrorism." Read that again. They opposed taking intelligence about al Qaeda because it might make America feel grateful to Syria. They would rather not have the intelligence than owe Syria a thank you. And here is the part that destroys the excuse that Israel had no choice. There were reports that the US would have welcomed Israeli talks with Syria. Ze'ev Schiff wrote in Ha'aretz in December 2003 that "in the opinion of American sources familiar with the thinking in the administration, it would have responded positively to an Israeli acceptance of Assad proposal. The United States is not looking in principle for a military confrontation with Damascus and is ready to let Assad get onto a positive track." Aluf Benn wrote in Ha'aretz a month later that "senior American officials" told the Israelis the US "will not object, should Israel choose to take up Syrian President Bashar Assad offer to resume negotiations." So America was open to peace with Syria. Israel was the one that said no. And then Israel blamed Bush for the no. this is the whole thing in one story. The president did not want this. His State Department opposed it. His CIA opposed it. He signed the bill on a Friday night to hide it. He told the Pentagon not to plan war with Syria. The neocons wanted to reject al Qaeda intelligence rather than owe Syria a thank you. And the only reason America was confronting Syria at all was because Israel wanted the confrontation and the lobby delivered it. Bush knew. He signed anyway. That is how the system works. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: The confrontation with Syria did not make America safer. It made things worse. And the Israel lobby kept pushing it. Results of the policy, according to the book. Syria stopped providing Washington with intelligence about al Qaeda. Assad did little to help the US shut down the insurgency in Iraq. He may have been trying to keep it going, because keeping the US bogged down in Baghdad made it less likely America would go after Syria. Damascus continued to support Hezbollah in Lebanon and formed a tacit alliance with Iran. That made it harder to keep peace in Lebanon and harder to stop Iran from getting nuclear weapons. None of this was good for the United States. In December 2006 the bipartisan Iraq Study Group called on Bush to "actively engage" with Syria in "diplomatic dialogue, without preconditions." That same month four US senators visited Damascus to talk with Assad. In April 2007 Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi led a bipartisan delegation to Syria, including Tom Lantos and Henry Waxman, both with strong pro-Israel credentials. But Israeli leaders, determined to hold the Golan Heights, had no interest in a cooperative US-Syria relationship. The most powerful groups in the lobby shared that view. They worked hard, and so far successfully, to keep the Bush administration from pursuing a more cooperative relationship with Assad. And here is the quote that says everything. After the 2006 Lebanon war, Meyrav Wurmser, who ran the Center for Middle East Policy at the Hudson Institute, said there was much anger toward Israel among her neoconservative colleagues "over the fact that Israel did not fight against the Syrians. Instead of Israel fighting against Hizbullah, many parts of the American administration believe that Israel should have fought against the real enemy, which is Syria and not Hizbullah." Read that again. The neoconservatives in the American administration were angry that Israel fought Hezbollah instead of Syria. They called Syria the real enemy. That was not an American assessment. That was the assessment of people whose foreign policy was organized around what Israel wanted. The book conclusion was blunt. "Without the lobby influence, there would have been no Syria Accountability Act and U.S. policy toward Damascus would have been more in line with the American national interest." A different US policy might have produced a Syrian-Israeli peace treaty by now. That treaty would have enshrined Israel legitimacy, reduced support for Hamas, Hezbollah, and Islamic Jihad, and made Israel more secure. Instead the lobby got its confrontation, and everyone lost. this is the whole pattern. The lobby pushed a policy that helped Israel keep land it took. The policy backfired and hurt America. The lobby did not change course. It pushed harder. And when a bipartisan group like the Iraq Study Group said try diplomacy, the lobby blocked it. When Pelosi went to Damascus, Israel humiliated her. When an American official said the road to Baghdad runs through Jerusalem, Israel said no it did not. Wurmser said the real enemy was Syria, not Hezbollah. That was not America talking. That was Israel talking through American officials. And we all paid for it. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: The Israel lobby is the network of pro-Israel groups in Washington. AIPAC is the biggest one. By 2006 George Bush was saying out loud that America would go to war with Iran to protect Israel. Not in private. In public speeches. March 20 2006, Cleveland: "The threat from Iran is, of course, their stated objective to destroy our strong ally Israel. That's a threat, a serious threat... I made it clear, I'll make it clear again, that we will use military might to protect our ally, Israel." A month earlier in an interview with Reuters he said: "we will rise to Israel's defense, if need be." And this was not one man. In April 2007 Senator John McCain said explicitly that he agreed with Bush that the United States had a responsibility to protect Israel from Iran. In a May 2007 interview with the Jerusalem Post he said it again. Barack Obama, Mitt Romney, Bill Richardson, and Sam Brownback gave similar comments. These were the people running for president. Then something strange happened. The Israel lobby got nervous about it. Spring 2006, the Forward reported: "Jewish community leaders have urged the White House to refrain from publicly pledging to defend Israel against possible Iranian hostilities." Why? Not because they opposed using American power for Israel. Because Bush's public statements "create an impression that the United States is considering a military option against Iran for the sake of Israel—and could lead to American Jews being blamed for any negative consequences of an American strike against Iran." Malcolm Hoenlein, executive vice chairman of the Conference of Presidents: "As much as we appreciate it, the question is whether it's beneficial to tie this to Israel." Israeli leaders felt the same. Prime Minister Ehud Olmert said that spring that he hoped pro-Israel groups would keep a low profile on Iran. "We don't want it to be about Israel," he said. That was the exact opposite of what the president of the United States was saying. When the president of the United States says he will go to war for Israel, and the Israel lobby asks him to stop saying it, that tells you everything. They know how it sounds. They know if Americans hear it out loud, they will ask why. So they want the war but they do not want the credit. Bush was giving them the war and they asked him to whisper. That is not a lobby with nothing to hide. That is a lobby that knows exactly what it is doing. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # Iran # MiddleEast # HumanRights

ARCHIVE: Mid-March 2007. Congress was working on a Pentagon spending bill. Some members wanted to add a provision. The provision was simple. President Bush would have to get Congress approval before attacking Iran. This was a popular measure. After the Iraq war disaster, nobody wanted another war started on a president word alone. The measure was consistent with Congress constitutional authority to declare war. It looked likely to pass. AIPAC opposed it. AIPAC is the biggest pro-Israel lobby group in Washington. It saw the provision as taking the military option against Iran off the table. So it went to work in the halls of Congress. With the help of a handful of pro-Israel representatives, Gary Ackerman, Eliot Engel, and Shelley Berkley, the provision was removed from the spending bill. One month later Congressman Michael Capuano was asked why the language on Iran was stripped out. He answered with one word: "AIPAC." Congressman Dennis Kucinich gave the same answer. One word. That is all it took. Not a debate. Not a vote. A lobby group walked into Congress and removed the requirement that the president ask Congress before starting a war. And the members of Congress who wanted it could not stop it. this is the single clearest example of the lobby overriding the constitutional process. The Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war. AIPAC took that power away from them on Iran. Not by amending the Constitution. By making a phone call and getting the provision pulled from a spending bill. And when a congressman was asked why, he just said the name. Everyone knew. Nobody could stop it. That is not lobbying. That is a veto over the American war powers. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # Iran # MiddleEast # HumanRights

ARCHIVE: 1995. Iran wanted better relations with America. So it did something clever. It chose Conoco, an American oil company, to develop the Sirri oil fields. Iran picked Conoco over several other foreign bidders on purpose. It was a signal. A friendly overture. The Israel lobby killed it. By mid-1994 the Israeli government had already asked AIPAC to move. Trita Parsi reports: "At the behest of the Israeli government, AIPAC drafted and circulated a 74-page paper in Washington arguing that Iran was not only a threat to Israel, but also to the United States and the West." Kenneth Pollack: "The right, AIPAC, the Israelis were all screaming for new sanctions on Iran." Senator Alfonse D'Amato introduced a bill in January 1995 to end all economic links with Iran. With, according to Pollack, "some help from the Israelis." The Clinton administration opposed it and it stalled. Then Conoco happened. Clinton killed the deal on March 14 1995. One day later he issued an executive order banning American companies from helping Iran develop its oil fields. Clinton later said that "one of the most effective opponents" of the Conoco deal was Edgar Bronfman Sr., the former head of the World Jewish Congress. AIPAC also played a key role in scuttling it. On May 6 Clinton issued a second executive order banning all trade and financial investment with Iran. He called Iran an "unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security, foreign policy, and economy of the United States." He had announced that step one week earlier in a speech to the World Jewish Congress. Pollack called the decision to kill Conoco and issue those orders "a major demonstration of our support for Israel." And here is the part that should make Americans angry. Although Israel was behind the American decision to cut economic ties with Iran, Israel did not pass any laws barring Israeli-Iranian trade. Israelis kept buying Iranian goods through third parties. America cut off its own companies. Israel did not cut off its own. The executive orders were not enough for the lobby. A. M. Rosenthal wrote in the New York Times: "The only problem with executive orders is that what the President giveth he can canceleth." So AIPAC acted. Parsi reports: "on its own initiative, AIPAC revised" the D'Amato bill "and convinced the New York Senator to reintroduce it in 1996—with AIPAC proposed changes." The bill became the Iran-Libya Sanctions Act. It punished any foreign company investing more than $40 million in Iranian or Libyan oil. It infuriated America European allies. The House passed it 415 to 0 on June 19 1996. The Senate passed it by unanimous consent one month later. Clinton signed it on August 5. Pollack: "much of the executive branch hated the D'Amato bill. In fact, for many, hated was too mild a word." But Clinton domestic policy advisers thought it would be "sheer stupidity" not to endorse it. Clinton was up for reelection in three months. Ze'ev Schiff of Ha'aretz: "Israel is but a tiny element in the big scheme, but one should not conclude that it cannot influence those within the beltway." James Schlesinger, who held several cabinet posts: "It is scarcely possible to overstate the influence of Israel supporters on our policies in the Middle East." One more thing. The oil lobby did not want this. Conoco wanted the deal. The oil industry opposed the sanctions bill. Dick Cheney at Halliburton publicly opposed the sanctions in the 1990s. Oil was steamrolled by AIPAC on every decision. this kills two myths at once. First, the myth that oil drives American Middle East policy. The oil companies wanted to do business with Iran and they lost. Second, the myth that Congress writes its own laws. AIPAC wrote this one. On its own initiative. At the behest of the Israeli government. And then Israel kept buying Iranian goods through third parties while America cut off its own companies. So Israel got the sanctions it wanted on American business and kept its own trade. That is not a partnership. That is a foreign government writing American law and exempting itself from it. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # Iran # MiddleEast # HumanRights

ARCHIVE: May 23 1997. Mohammad Khatami was elected president of Iran. He was more enthusiastic than his predecessor about improving relations with the West and the United States in particular. He made conciliatory remarks in his inaugural speech on August 4 and in his first press conference on December 14. Then on January 7 1998 he gave a lengthy CNN interview. He expressed respect for "the great American people" and "their great civilization." He said Iran did not "aim to destroy or undermine the American government." He regretted the 1979 embassy takeover. He called for "a crack in this wall of mistrust to prepare for a change and create an opportunity to study a new situation." He did not rule out an Israeli state in historic Palestine. He declared that "terrorism should be condemned in all its forms and manifestations." He denounced terrorism against Israelis. Other Iranian spokesmen soon echoed Iran willingness to accept Israel if it reached an agreement with the Palestinians. The Clinton administration responded. After checking with Israel and key figures in Congress, it made small gestures. Clinton and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright made contrite remarks about past Western conduct. The US eased visa restrictions. Even Martin Indyk, the architect of dual containment, said: "The United States has made it clear repeatedly that we have nothing against an Islamic government in Iran... We are ready for a dialogue." Then Israel moved to stop it. Ha'aretz reported that "Israel has expressed its concern to Washington at reports of an impending change of policy by the United States towards Iran." Prime Minister Netanyahu "has asked AIPAC... to act vigorously in Congress to prevent such a policy shift." AIPAC did as Netanyahu asked. Gary Sick, one of America leading experts on Iran: "The gradual improvement of U.S.-Iran relations after the election of Khatami was not reflected in AIPAC positions. In fact, by early 1999 only AIPAC, the Iranian monarchists in exile and the terrorist Mojahedin-e Khalq persisted in their relentless insistence that little or nothing had changed in Iran." Even when the Israeli ambassador to the US said in spring 2000 that it would be acceptable for Clinton to allow food and medical supplies to be exported to Iran, AIPAC still campaigned against the legislation. When Clinton lifted the ban on caviar, Persian rugs, and pistachios, AIPAC did not object. But the Anti-Defamation League and the Conference of Presidents did. Clinton got his way on the small stuff. But the US never made a serious effort to grasp the hand Khatami extended. Ephraim Sneh, one of Israel leading hawks on Iran, explained why: "We were against it [United States–Iran dialogue]... because the interest of the US did not coincide with ours." He said it out loud. The US interest did not coincide with Israel interest. So Israel blocked the US from pursuing its own interest. Sneh quote is the whole book in one sentence. A former Israeli general and cabinet minister admits on the record that Israel blocked America from talking to Iran because the talks were good for America but not for Israel. That is not a partnership. That is one country using another country against its own interest. And the American president went along with it. He checked with Israel before making gestures to Iran. He let AIPAC kill the opening. And the chance for peace in 1998 was lost. We are still paying for that today. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # Iran # MiddleEast # HumanRights

ARCHIVE: Iran helped America after 9/11. Then America thanked Iran by putting it in the axis of evil. Then Iran tried again with a full grand bargain. America said no. Israel and the lobby were a big reason why. Fall 2001. Iran helped the United States topple the Taliban. It provided advice on targets to strike in Afghanistan. It facilitated US cooperation with the Northern Alliance. It helped with search-and-rescue missions. After the war Tehran helped Washington put a friendly government in place in Kabul. At the same time Iran President Khatami made it clear once again that he wanted to improve relations with the United States. He saw events in Afghanistan as a major step in that direction. There was substantial support inside the CIA and the State Department for taking Khatami at his word and normalizing relations. The neoconservatives inside and outside the administration opposed it. They favored getting tough with Iran and they carried the day with Bush and Cheney. In his State of the Union address in late January 2002 Bush rewarded Iran for its cooperation in Afghanistan by including it in the infamous "axis of evil." He made clear in the following months that although he was focused on Iraq he would eventually try to topple the Iranian government too. Iran tried again in spring 2003. Khatami said he was willing to negotiate on Iran nuclear program so that it would be readily transparent that "there are no Iranian endeavors to develop or possess WMD." On terrorism he said Iran would end "any material support to Palestinian opposition groups (Hamas, Jihad, etc.)" and put "pressure on these organizations to stop violent action against civilians" within Israel 1967 borders. On Hezbollah Iran goal would be to make it "a mere political organization within Lebanon." Khatami indicated "acceptance" of the 2002 Saudi peace initiative, which he made clear meant acceptance of a two-state solution. Iran would help stabilize Iraq. In return Khatami wanted the US to remove Iran from the axis of evil and take away the threat to use military force. Sanctions had to go. And Iran wanted "full access to peaceful nuclear technology." In essence Khatami was offering a solution that had all the ingredients of a grand bargain. On nukes. On Hamas. On Hezbollah. On Israel. On Iraq. Everything. The offer came in May 2003, just after the US appeared to score a stunning victory in Iraq and Afghanistan. US prestige and leverage were at their peak. Iran sense of vulnerability was acute. It was the ideal time to cut a deal. Bush paid hardly any attention to it. US officials were ordered not to pursue it. Why? Israel was pressing the Bush administration hard at that point to take aim at Iran. So were the neoconservatives and others in the lobby. And America favorable position made Bush more inclined to dictate rather than deal. this is the moment that proves the whole argument. Iran was not just talking. It was putting everything on the table. Nukes. Hamas. Hezbollah. Two states. Iraq. In return it wanted the threat of war removed and sanctions lifted. That is the deal America says it wants today. In 2003 Iran offered it and America said no. Because Israel did not want the deal. Because the neocons did not want the deal. So instead of a deal we got two decades of confrontation, an Iranian nuclear program that is now at the threshold, and the risk of a war that nobody can win. That is what the lobby bought with all that influence. Not peace. Not security. Just an endless crisis. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # Iran # MiddleEast # HumanRights

Spring 2002: AIPAC promoted legislation to formally place Syria on the "axis of evil." Engel introduced the Syria Accountability Act. It threatened sanctions unless Syria withdrew from Lebanon, gave up its WMD, and stopped supporting terrorism. It also called for Syria and Lebanon to take concrete steps to make peace with Israel. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported the bill was "framed by some of Israel best friends in Congress" and that its "most avid proponent in the administration" was Elliott Abrams. The Bush administration opposed the bill in spring 2002. Two reasons. It might undermine the push for the Iraq war. And it might make Damascus stop giving Washington intelligence about al Qaeda. Congress put it on the back burner. Then Baghdad fell in April 2003. The lobby renewed the campaign. And now they wanted regime change, not behavior change. Paul Wolfowitz: "there has got to be regime change in Syria." Richard Perle: the message to other regimes is a two-word message. "You're next." The Defense Policy Board headed by Perle pushed a hard line against Syria. John Bolton prepared to tell Congress in mid-July 2003 that Syria WMD programs were a serious threat and had to be dealt with soon. The CIA and other agencies objected. They said Bolton was inflating the danger. The administration blocked his testimony. Bolton went anyway in September and called Syria a growing threat. April 2003 op-ed barrage: Yossi Klein Halevi in the LA Times "Next, Turn the Screws on Syria." Frank Gaffney in the Washington Times calling for "whatever techniques are necessary—including military force—to effect behavior modification and/or regime change in Damascus." Zev Chafets in the New York Daily News "Terror-Friendly Syria Needs a Change, Too." Lawrence Kaplan in the New Republic saying Assad was a serious threat to America. August 2003: Engel and a group of New York politicians and Jewish leaders met Sharon in his Jerusalem office for ninety minutes. Sharon complained the US was not pressuring Syria enough. He thanked Engel for sponsoring the bill. He made clear he strongly favored continuing efforts to push it in Congress. The following month Engel announced he was "fed up with the administration's maneuvering on Syria" and pushed the bill again. With AIPAC full support he rounded up votes. Bush could no longer hold Congress back. The bill passed 398 to 4 in the House and 89 to 4 in the Senate.
